proposition: Ninety-nine is not a fact about forts. It is a general-purpose Rigvedic quantity that forts are one of several kinds of thing to take.
evidence_for: The náva- 1 + navatí- expression co-occurs in 19 stanzas; on a strict reading, where the expression yields 99 as the quantity of the object, 16. Forts take it in 6 - well under half either way. The rest are rivers (1.32.14, 10.104.8), Vr̥tras (1.84.13), arms (2.14.4), horses (4.48.4), a serpent's coils (5.29.6), ramparts (6.47.2), unnamed broken things (9.61.1), gifts (10.39.10) and the mighty (10.49.8). Nothing links that list except the number. RV 10.104.8 carries the expression counting streams AND the epithet pūrbhít 'fort-breaker' in one stanza. The twelve non-fort uses span seven books (1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10) and at least five Arnold strata, so they are not a local mannerism of one book or poet. Ninety-nine is also not modal: nine passages state a śatá- count against six for 99 (DJ-015).
evidence_against: The number does not float free of narrative: 99 and 100 sort to Divodāsa, Atithigva and Śambara, while 7 goes with Purukutsa and the Pūru in all four of their passages (PUR4J finding 5). Ornament does not sort by story, so a quantity used for nine kinds of object is still doing something when it is chosen. And the denominator is small: 16 to 19 stanzas supports a claim about usage, not a law.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does not establish that no Rigvedic fort count records anything historical - a formulaic number can be attached to a remembered event, and one of the six could be. It does not establish WHY ninety-nine: a decimal-adjacent maximum, a one-short-of-a-hundred completion (two of the six add 'the hundredth'), and a stock epic quantity are all live and none is tested here.
falsifier: Falsified by a count outside the stock - a 23 or a 41 - attached to a fort, which would show the corpus can state an arbitrary number and chooses not to. Weakened if the six fort uses prove separable from the rest by stratum or dialect. The book-and-stratum spread reported above is a crude test and a finer one could still find structure.
notes: This SUPERSEDES nothing in PUR4J-I-01, which reached a compatible conclusion from one control case. It widens the base and is recorded separately because the widening is this unit's. AMENDED after adversarial review: the earlier row said 'forts are 6 of 19 - under a third' without noting that three of the nineteen (1.53.9, 1.191.13, 10.98.10) do not yield 99 as the quantity of the object. The strict denominator is 16.

proposition: The gloss column of the pinned corpus carries no noun for 'brick' or 'city'; a translator inside the same corpus reads a púr- as a city at one locator and infers unfired brick at another; and the corpus applies its 'raw' word to a fort exactly once. None of the three settles what a púr- was built of, and the absence cannot be typed under §6 from anything retrieved here.
evidence_for: No lemma in the gloss column is glossed 'brick' or 'city' against a 91.7% lemma / 78.98% token denominator, and both are nouns, so the nominal coverage of the column carries the absence (DJ-008). The column's own entry for púr- is an earthwork - 'Wall aus Steinen und Lehm, Verschanzung, Palisade' - not a city. 67.5% of simplex tokens are accusative and 3.6% locative: the commonest thing a púr does is be the object of a verb of breaking (DJ-006). The corpus has abundant settlement vocabulary that is NOT púr- (DJ-012).
evidence_against: THREE ITEMS, ALL FORCED BY ADVERSARIAL REVIEW, AND TWO OF THEM WEAKER THAN THIS ROW FIRST CLAIMED. (1) At RV 1.173.10 Renou renders pū́rpati- 'maître de la cité' - a púr read as a CITY by a translator inside the pinned corpus, unbracketed and in his own voice (DJ-013). At RV 2.35.6 he has 'forteresses (en briques) crues', but 'en briques' is his own bracketed supplement and the Sanskrit carries no material word; it is evidence about his reading, not about the text. (2) RV 2.35.6 applies āmá- 'raw, uncooked' to a púr - the only place the cooked/raw pair is applied to a structure (DJ-009). The pair itself is culinary and this row earlier called it 'the fired/unfired opposition brick technology turns on', which the passages do not support. (3) RV 6.2.7 'like an old man in a fort' and RV 9.107.10 'as a body of troops enters the fort' are similes, and a simile draws on what its audience finds ordinary, so both PRESUPPOSE the inhabited fort the corpus never asserts (DJ-007). pū́rpati- is itself inside a simile and is one token (DJ-014), which cuts both ways.
what_it_does_not_establish: It does not establish that Rigvedic púr- were small, temporary or non-urban. It does not establish that brick was unknown to the composers, and after DJ-009 and DJ-013 it should not be read as evidence that it was. It does not settle whether púr- and the Harappan citadel are the same object: that is HYP-J-001, and the answer there is that this repository cannot tell. It also does not establish anything about what the corpus says about BUILDING: the gloss column has zero coverage of verb roots (0 of 700, 19.4% of tokens), so no negative about an action is available from it (DJ-009, BF-018).
falsifier: Falsified in the deflationary direction by a noun glossed 'brick' or 'city' in a lexicon independent of the Zurich column, which would also show the single-source dependency was doing the work. Moved substantially by Sāyaṇa or any pre-modern commentary on the ten material passages. Moved in the other direction by a second passage applying pakvá- or āmá- to a structure - RV 2.35.6 is currently the only one, established by enumerating all 36 tokens and their agreement partners (DJ-009), so this falsifier is a search over a closed set that has been run, not an outstanding one. An earlier version of this column said that survey 'was not run', which contradicted DJ-009 in the same commit.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/domain-j-measurements.csv DJ-006 to DJ-009 and DJ-012 to DJ-014; 03-REGISTERS/HYPOTHESIS-ELIGIBILITY.csv HYP-J-001
notes: THE PROPOSITION OF THIS ROW HAS NOW BEEN REWRITTEN THREE TIMES, EVERY TIME AWAY FROM THE SAME CONVENIENT CONCLUSION, AND TWICE THE CORRECTION ITSELF OVERSHOT. Draft 1 asserted 'no word for brick, no word for city, therefore not a Harappan city'; corrected by the two similes (BF-016). Draft 2 read 'no positive lexical evidence ... and no evidence that it was not', which was false in its own corpus: Renou and the pakvá-/āmá- pair had been retrieved and not read (BF-017). Draft 3 - this row's previous version - overcorrected TOWARD the thesis: it presented Renou's bracketed 'briques' as though the text stated a material, called a culinary opposition 'the fired/unfired opposition brick technology turns on', carried a negative about building that the gloss column structurally cannot support, and closed with 'cannot be read that way AT ALL' - an absolute of exactly the kind struck from DJ-011 one round earlier. The pattern across all three: the checks that would have settled each draft were free, and each draft disclosed a limitation instead of running one. BF-017, BF-018.

proposition: The English word 'fort' is not a translation of a Rigvedic category. It is a bracket that several Sanskrit words fall into and out of, and where the bracket is contested the translators are contested too.
evidence_for: The great majority of the 21 durgá- tokens denote difficult ground or peril rather than a fortification, and the recurrent construction is a prayer to be carried across one (DJ-011). dehī́- 'Aufwurf, Damm, Wall' - an earth-heap from √dih 'smear, plaster up' - takes the same ninety-nine expression and the same opponent as púr- but sits outside the register by an etymological rule (DJ-005). The gloss column's púr- is an earthwork or palisade, not a city. Translators diverge on the same word within one corpus: at RV 2.35.6 Griffith has 'forts unwrought', Geldner 'rohen Burgen' and Renou 'forteresses (en briques) crues' - where 'en briques' is Renou's own bracketed supplement and not in the Sanskrit; at RV 1.173.10 Griffith 'some city's lord', Geldner 'Burgherren', Renou 'maître de la cité', all three unbracketed (DJ-013).
evidence_against: THE ABSOLUTE FORM OF THE durgá- CLAIM IS FALSE AND THE FALSIFIER THIS ROW DECLARED HAS FIRED. At RV 5.34.7 all three of Griffith, Geldner and Grassmann render durgá- as a fortified place people hold out in, and at RV 5.54.4 they disagree with each other. Two further passages are unresolved (RV 4.28.3, 7.25.2). The durgá- base is also thinner than 21 suggests: six tokens are one refrain and RV 7.60.12 and 7.61.7 are word for word identical, so there are at most 15 distinct formulations. Separately, the earlier version of this row said grā́ma- is 'a moving war-band in Grassmann's Rigvedic gloss' - false twice over: the gloss is the Zurich column's, not Grassmann's, and it reads '... wehrhafte Mannschaft einer Siedlung, Dorfgemeinde, bewohnter Platz', carrying the village sense the row denied by truncating the quotation (DJ-012).
what_it_does_not_establish: It does not establish what any of these words did mean, only that the English bracket does not carry evenly across them. It does not license replacing 'fort' with 'earthwork' as a new default gloss - that would repeat the error in the other direction. It does not establish that durgá- is never a fortification in the Rigveda; RV 5.34.7 is evidence that it sometimes is.
falsifier: For durgá-, the strong form is ALREADY FALSIFIED at RV 5.34.7. The surviving weak form - that difficult ground is the dominant sense - would be falsified by a majority of the remaining passages reading as fortifications under a lexicon independent of the Zurich column, or by a pre-modern commentary reading them so.
notes: §7 names 'fort' among the inherited English categories to audit before use. This row is the audit at the level of the category. It is PROVISIONAL and its strongest single item has been withdrawn: the claim that no durgá- is ever held was the load-bearing anti-Nandi result, it was shipped VERIFIED, and it was contradicted by a translation file the unit had already retrieved and cited. BF-017 and RA-020.
